newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban launch attack on Panjsher Valley.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban launch attack on Panjsher Valley.

text.p: Afghanistan's hardline Islamist Taleban militia launched an attack on the Panjsher Valley stronghold of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Mass Masood on Saturday, witnesses said.
There was no immediate word on how successful the assault had been on the narrow entrance to a rocky gorge that leads into the valley from the village of Golbahar at its mouth.
At 10 minute intervals, the Taleban fired volleys of a dozen rockets from truck-mounted multiple launchers at Masood positions on the narrow crests of the sides of the gorge.
About 50 black-turbanned Taleban warriors scaled one steep, rocky side of the outside of the gorge towards the top where the rockets were landing.

Taleban fighters said the volleys of rockets began in the pre-dawn darkness, but there was little sign of firing from Masood's men holding well-entrenched positions inside the winding gorge. A Taleban gun was firing up the gorge.

Taleban leaders had called on Masood to surrender or be cleared out of the valley to which he retreated in some chaos after the Sunni Moslem militia composed mainly of ethnic Pushtuns took Kabul a week ago in a lightning strike.
There has been no word of any reply from Masood, who defended the valley populated by ethnic Tajiks many times against Soviet forces who backed the communist government in Kabul during the 1980s.

Soviet forces used bombers and mass helicopter landings in their vain attempts to capture the Panjsher in battles that gave Masood a reputation as one of the best guerrilla generals in the 13-year war against the communist government.
He became defence minister in the guerrilla government that ousted that led by president Najibullah in 1992, three years after Soviet forces quit Afghanistan.
Since his retreat to the Panjsher, Masood has been working intensively to organise its defence against the Taleban, his men say.

They have used dynamite to bring landslides down across the narrow road that runs alongside a swift-flowing river into the Panjsher in an effort to seal off a valley where Masood has stockpiled plenty of fuel, ammunition and food, his men say.

He imposed a state of emergency on the valley and ordered all non-combatants to leave it, sending a stream of women, children and the elderly clambering to safety along a narrow, rock strewn path that clings to one side of the treeless gorge.
The Taleban have none of the bombers the Soviet forces used before attacks on the Panjsher and are not known to have used helicopter landings in previous battles.
The movement has gained control of about three-quarters of the country in the two years since it was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan.
One Western former military officer who trekked into the Panjsher earlier this week said he did not believe the Taleban fighters could take it.

The gorge winds into the valley and the only routes into it are either over the tops of the ridges or along the path the refugees used. Masood's men had a series of well-entrenched positions along it.
The landslides across the road effectively bar the use of tanks, which the Taleban have moved up to Golbahar, the former army officer said.

The Taleban leadership has said the militia would deal with Masood before dealing with another potential foe, Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who controls six northern provinces from the city of Mazar-i-Sharif.
The Taleban say they have no quarrel with Dostum, a former communist general who switched sides just before Najibullah's government collapsed, and are prepared to negotiate with him.
There has been no firm word on negotiations so far. But Dostum has moved tanks and other heavy military equipment south of the Salang Tunnel, 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul.
The tunnel is a key choke point on the road from Kabul through the Hindu Kush mountain range to Mazar-i-Sharif and on to central Asia.

The Uzbeks, descended from the Mongols of Genghis Khan, are widely regarded as some of the best fighters in Afghanistan and practise a much more liberal version of Islam than the Taleban, who are committed to imposing a strict Islamic way of life.
One Uzbek officer told Reuters in the Salang Pass this week that Dostum's army was ready to fight the Taleban if they tried to force their way into the far north.
